units.title: High-throughput chains with modified gas models
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Opcode differential. For each opcode and call pattern the PoolManager relies on (TSTORE and TLOAD including rollback on revert and clearing at transaction end, CALL with value, CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY, MCOPY, PUSH0, gas forwarding, calls to addresses without code, precompile dispatch), read this network's execution client source and find where it departs from Ethereum's behaviour.

code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10, 11 and 12 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Lead L-679. OPCODES.md records that 85,278 of 88,576 mined swap pairs match the single-step formulas of src/libraries/SwapMath.sol and SqrtPriceMath.sol, and that the rest were attributed to swaps that cross ticks or to unknown tick spacing, without being reproduced. The op-stack-eth unit of cycle 12 showed that four such Ink swaps were only a missing tick spacing (90) in tools/opdiff/replay.py. Close the residue on all 21 networks in state/networks.json. For each network collect a fresh window of Swap events of the PoolManager (at least 3,000 where the network has that many, plus the unmatched cases recorded in research/network-risk/opcodes/ and in the work directories of cycles 8 to 12 where they are kept). For every swap that the single-step formulas do not reproduce, obtain the pool key (fee, tick spacing, hooks) from the Initialize event of that pool id, read liquidity, slot0, fee growth and the tick bitmap words and initialized ticks from the parent block with eth_call on extsload (src/Extsload.sol) or eth_getStorageAt, and rerun the whole swap loop of src/libraries/Pool.sol swap() in Python step by step: every tick crossing, liquidityNet, the fee of each step, protocol fee, the lpFee override returned by a hook where the Swap event shows it. The result to check is the Swap event's amount0, amount1, sqrtPriceX96, liquidity, tick and fee, to the unit. Write a tool tools/opdiff/replay2.py that does this for any network and endpoint, keep raw outputs in your work directory, and report per network: swaps collected, matched by single step, matched by the full loop, set aside with the reason (hook that changes amounts through return deltas, several swaps on one pool in one block where the parent state is not the state before the swap, missing archive state), and unmatched. For swaps that share a block, order them by log index and carry the state forward, or use debug_traceTransaction where served. Any swap that stays unmatched after that is the result that matters most: give the transaction hash, the inputs, the expected and mined outputs, and which line of SwapMath, SqrtPriceMath, FullMath, TickMath or TickBitmap the difference points at.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10, 11 and 12 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Lead L-678 and L-670. On Monad (143), MegaETH (4326) and HyperEVM (999) the program that produces blocks is not the program that answers eth_call (Monad producers run compiled native code, the MegaETH sequencer and the HyperEVM validator are closed), so the pmdiff6 scripts of cycle 12 (research/network-risk/cycles/012/theme-bytecode-coverage.work, jumpmap-after.json lists every conditional jump with its source meaning) say nothing about producers for the 83 branches they newly cover. Find mined instances. From PoolManager logs and transactions in recent blocks (and older blocks where an archive endpoint serves them), find transactions that take each of these branches: clear() of an exact credit (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319), transferFrom and burn with a finite allowance and with the infinite allowance (src/ERC6909.sol), operator approvals, hooks with the return-delta permission bits (beforeSwapReturnDelta, afterSwapReturnDelta, afterAddLiquidityReturnDelta, afterRemoveLiquidityReturnDelta; src/libraries/Hooks.sol), hooks that call the PoolManager from inside a callback, dynamic fee pools with an lpFee override, donate, settleFor, mint and burn of claims, take of the native currency, swaps that hit the price limit, swaps with exact output, and swaps that end exactly on an initialized tick. Use debug_traceTransaction with callTracer where served (Monad serves it), event logs elsewhere. For each branch with at least one mined instance, rerun the transaction in tools/opdiff/pyevm.py from the parent block's state (prestateTracer, or eth_getStorageAt and eth_getCode at the parent block; cycles 11 and 12 left block-level simulators in cycles/011/theme-mined-liquidity.work and cycles/012/theme-mined-liquidity-2.work that you can reuse) and compare logs, return values of the PoolManager frames and the storage words the PoolManager wrote, to the unit. Report per network and per branch: instances found, instances rerun, matched, set aside with the reason, unmatched. Also list the branches for which no mined instance exists on a network, because those are the ones for which the producer has no evidence at all. Extend to Polygon (BlockSTM), Arbitrum One and Ethereum as controls only if time allows.

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10, 11 and 12 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Leads L-677, L-680, L-683, L-682 and L-673. The state users withdraw against is on rollups decided by a build other than the node. Cycle 12 (cycles/012/theme-proof-builds.research.json and its work directory, which holds a Python transcription of uint256 v1.3.2 with wasm and MIPS64 arithmetic) settled OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink, World Chain, Zora and Soneium and the Arbitrum wasm replay. Open parts. One, Nitro: both Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain endpoints report nitro v3.13.0-rc.9+b72783f, which no public tag carries. Read which go-ethereum fork commit the nitro master branch and the newest public v3.13 tags or release branches pin (submodule reference or go.mod), and in that commit read core/vm (jump destination cache and its key, contract.go, interpreter.go, instructions.go, the uint256 version) and the prefetcher: is the cache key always the hash of the analysed bytes, does a speculative StateDB write the shared cache, do entries survive a reorg or an EIP-7702 redelegation, and did any opcode handler change since the commit cycle 9 to 12 read (0e44603)? Two, Base: the portal respects game type 621, an AggregateVerifier (TEE image hash 0x73181275..., SP1 range program hash 0x3d3713d3...). Find the release that produces those hashes, the revm, revm-interpreter, ruint and alloy-primitives versions the range program embeds, whether keccak caching is linked on the zkVM target, and who can call challenge or prove. Three, Celo (42220) and X Layer (196): read on Ethereum by eth_call the respected game type and gameImpls of each DisputeGameFactory, the prestate or verification key, and the program and integer library behind it. Four, kona-client 1.9.0 on MIPS64 (OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink): find which routines ruint 1.20.0 uses for 64x64 to 128 products and 128 by 64 divisions on a target without native 128 bit arithmetic (compiler-builtins __multi3, __udivti3, __umodti3, or ruint's own algorithms: read ruint src/algorithms/div and mul, and compiler-builtins' int/specialized_div_rem and mul), transcribe them to Python and run tools/opdiff/targeted.py and battery.py vectors for MUL, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, ADDMOD, MULMOD, EXP and the shifts through the transcription against the expected words; plant a fault to show the check can fail. For each part say whether any opcode the PoolManager runs could give another result in the proof build than on the node, and whether an ordinary account could use that (a disputable honest root delays or blocks withdrawals of pool funds; a provable wrong root takes them).

The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10, 11 and 12 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Leads L-681, L-684 and L-669. Two questions about what a client does around the opcodes the PoolManager runs. One, instruction overrides: for every network whose client is a revm fork or wraps the interpreter (Arc arc-node crates/evm/src/opcode.rs, Tempo, MegaETH mega-evm, X Layer xlayer-reth, Celo celo-reth, World Chain, Base, op-revm, reth-bsc, Monad's interpreter and compiler opcode tables, HyperEVM nanoreth and what is documented of hl-node, bor, BSC geth, avalanchego libevm hooks, Nitro), list every opcode handler, gas function or call hook the client replaces, wraps or adds relative to stock Ethereum at the release the endpoint reports, as a table with file and line. For each replaced handler say whether the PoolManager runtime executes that opcode (build/PoolManager.json; CALL with value at src/types/Currency.sol:48, token calls at :73, BALANCE and SELFBALANCE at :92, STATICCALL in hooks and extsload callers, TSTORE and TLOAD, SSTORE, LOG, MCOPY, RETURNDATACOPY, KECCAK256, GAS, CALLVALUE, CALLER, ADDRESS, CODESIZE, EXTCODESIZE is not used) and whether the replacement can return another value, another success flag, other return data or another amount of gas left than stock for the PoolManager's operands. Arc is the one network known to override an opcode handler (SELFDESTRUCT, finding F-032) and no unit has read its override set as a whole; do Arc first and completely. Two, callee gas: hook calls and native transfers forward all remaining gas (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, src/types/Currency.sol:48 and :73). Cycle 12 found that Monad's staking precompile at 0x1000 consumes all forwarded gas when a call fails, and that 0x1000 is a system contract on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain. For every network list the precompiles, predeploys and system contracts that consume all forwarded gas on failure or that cost gas out of proportion (stateful precompiles on Avalanche, Tempo, Arc, Celo, HyperEVM read precompiles at 0x0800 and CoreWriter, Monad staking, Arbitrum ArbSys family, OP Stack predeploys, MegaETH system contracts), by eth_call with from set to the PoolManager address and a gas cap, measuring gas used. Then decide whether an ordinary account can make one of them the recipient of a take or a native transfer, a hook address or a token address inside a transaction that a victim sends through a normal router (a victim swapping on an existing honest pool), as opposed to the attacker's own transaction, where it is harmless. Report anything that would make a victim's swap or liquidity removal fail or cost far more on one network than on Ethereum.
